question: The Polish road transport sector has been at the forefront of international transport in the European Union for many years and is one of the pillars of the functioning of the common market and European supply chains. Polish hauliers carry out a significant proportion of road transport operations within the EU, ensuring the competitiveness of the European economy and the logistical safety of Member States.

However, transport companies operating in the EU, in particular in the SME sector, are under strong pressure due to the impact of the war in Ukraine, the economic slowdown in Germany, rising fuel costs, financing, wages and road tolls.

The activity of Ukrainian hauliers also poses an additional challenge, since they operate outside the provisions of the mobility package and benefit from lower operating costs, such as for fuel, when entering the EU, including Poland. As of January 2026, 1 234 Polish transport companies have disappeared and hundreds more are on the brink of bankruptcy.
This is why hauliers are warning that the Commission needs to act. In connection to the above: 1.
Is the Commission planning additional support programmes for EU hauliers, particularly from border countries?
Does the Commission intend to review the rules on the liberalisation of road transport between the EU and Ukraine, the effects of which contribute to the collapse of Polish and European hauliers?
Does the Commission envisage any safeguarding mechanisms to ensure a level playing field between EU and Ukrainian hauliers?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.8.2026) The Commission is well aware of the concerns raised by the Polish haulage companies in relation to the Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine on the Carriage of Freight by Road (‘the Agreement’)1.

As indicated in the reply to Question E-002109/2025, any potential abuse or unfair competition is now prevented following modifications to the Agreement made in 2024. Road transport operations from and to Ukraine represent, on average, only a small proportion of the business of EU hauliers. Ukrainian trucks entering the EU must also comply with international road transport regulations and safety standards.

Against this background, the Commission has so far not identified any major disturbance on the EU haulage market arising from the rights granted to Ukrainian haulage undertakings under the Agreement. The Commission has launched a study on the impact of the Agreement on the road transport market which will be delivered by 30 November 2026.

The Commission is also assessing if satisfactory progress is made on the alignment of Ukrainian legislation with the relevant EU acquis to ensure a level playing field with EU haulage operators. Any decision to further prolong the Agreement after 31 March 2027 will be subject to satisfactory progress made by Ukraine on alignment with the EU acquis and will be informed by the results of the study2.

The Commission has approved, under EU State aid rules, a EUR 1.5 billion (PLN 6.4 billion) Polish scheme to provide State-supported reinsurance of insurance for transport on the territory of Ukraine3.
1 Agreement between the European Union and Ukraine on the carriage of freight by road (OJ L 179, 6.7.2022,
